title: Arduino and Robotics
description: From the first blinking LED to a robot that follows a line on its own: basic electronics, inputs and outputs, PWM, sensors, motors and control — all on a simulated Arduino.

ard-01-pisca-led.title: Blink: the "Hello, world" of electronics
ard-01-pisca-led.theory:
# What is an Arduino?

The **Arduino Uno** is a small board with a **microcontroller**: a tiny computer that runs **a single program** (the *sketch*) forever, from the moment it gets power. It has **pins** — the little holes along its sides — that can **switch things on and off** (outputs) or **read things** (inputs).

- Digital pins: **0 to 13**. Each one is either `HIGH` (5 volts) or `LOW` (0 volts).
- Analog pins: **A0 to A5** (we'll see them later).

# The structure of every sketch

Every Arduino program has two mandatory functions:

```
void setup() {
  // runs ONCE, when the board powers up
}

void loop() {
  // runs again and again, forever
}
```

# The LED and the resistor (Ohm's law)

An **LED** (light-emitting diode) only lets current flow in one direction: the **long** leg (anode, +) goes to the pin and the **short** one (cathode, −) goes to GND. It needs a **resistor** in series, otherwise the current gets too high and the LED (or the pin) burns out.

**Ohm's law** says: **V = R × I** (voltage = resistance × current). The pin gives 5 V and the LED "uses up" about 2 V, so 3 V are left across the resistor. For a safe current of 15 mA (0.015 A):

**R = V / I = 3 / 0.015 = 200 Ω** → we use the next standard value up, **220 Ω**, which lets 3 / 220 ≈ **14 mA** through.

Each Arduino pin can take an **absolute maximum of 40 mA**; the recommended limit is **20 mA**. That's why the resistor must never be left out.

Pin **13** already has an LED on the board itself (`LED_BUILTIN`), and in our circuit a red LED is connected to it.

# The three commands of this lesson

- `pinMode(13, OUTPUT);` — says that pin 13 will be an **output**. Without it, the pin stays an input and the LED barely lights up!
- `digitalWrite(13, HIGH);` — puts 5 V on the pin: the LED **turns on**. `LOW` turns it off.
- `delay(1000);` — waits **1000 milliseconds** (1 second) doing nothing.
ard-01-pisca-led.task: Make the LED on pin 13 blink: **on for 1 second, off for 1 second**, forever. Remember to set the pin as an output in `setup()`.
hints: In setup() write pinMode(13, OUTPUT); — this turns pin 13 into an output.
loop() has 4 lines: digitalWrite(13, HIGH); delay(1000); digitalWrite(13, LOW); delay(1000);
Don't forget the semicolon at the end of every command, and write HIGH and LOW in capitals.
checks: The LED is on during the first second
The LED is off between 1 s and 2 s
The LED turns on again (the loop repeats)
Pin 13 is HIGH at 4.5 s

ard-03-pwm-fade.title: PWM: the LED that fades in and out
ard-03-pwm-fade.theory:
# Digital has only two levels… or does it?

A digital pin can only give 0 V or 5 V. So how do we get an LED at **half brightness**? The trick is called **PWM** (*Pulse Width Modulation*).

# How PWM works

The pin switches on and off **very fast**: about **490 times per second** (490 Hz) on pin 9, and 980 Hz on pins 5 and 6. What changes is **how long** it stays on in each cycle — the **duty cycle**:

- 0% on → LED off
- 25% on → dim
- 50% on → half brightness
- 100% on → full brightness

Our eyes can't see such fast blinking and only perceive the **average**. The average voltage is: **V_avg = 5 V × duty**. At 50%, it's as if the LED were getting 2.5 V.

# analogWrite

```
analogWrite(9, 128);   // 128 out of 255 ≈ on 50% of the time
```

The value goes from **0** (always off) to **255** (always on). Why 255? Because the chip's timer uses **8 bits**, and 2⁸ = 256 values (0 to 255).

**Note:** only the pins marked with **~** have PWM on the Uno: **3, 5, 6, 9, 10 and 11**. That's why this lesson's LED is on pin 9.

# The for loop

To raise the brightness little by little, we use `for`:

```
for (int brilho = 0; brilho <= 255; brilho += 5) {
  analogWrite(9, brilho);
  delay(10);
}
```

It reads: "start with brilho = 0; while brilho ≤ 255, run the block and then add 5". That's 52 steps of 10 ms ≈ half a second to light up. To fade out, write another `for` counting **down** (`brilho -= 5`).

(*brilho* is Portuguese for "brightness".)
ard-03-pwm-fade.task: Make the LED on pin **9** fade in smoothly from 0 to 255 (steps of **5** every **10 ms**) and then fade out smoothly from 255 to 0 the same way, repeating forever.
hints: Use analogWrite(LED, brilho); and not digitalWrite — only analogWrite produces in-between values.
Going up: for (int brilho = 0; brilho <= 255; brilho += 5) { ... }
Going down: for (int brilho = 255; brilho >= 0; brilho -= 5) { ... } — with the same delay(10) inside.
checks: At 0.25 s the LED is at medium brightness (rising)
Pin 9 is doing PWM (an in-between value)
At about 0.5 s the brightness reaches the maximum
At 0.78 s the brightness is medium again (falling)
At about 1 s the LED is almost off

ard-04-potenciometro.title: Potentiometer and analogRead: a dimmer
ard-04-potenciometro.theory:
# Analog signals

Many things in the real world aren't just "on/off": the position of a volume knob, the light in the room, the temperature. They vary **continuously**. For these, the Arduino has pins **A0 to A5**, connected to an **ADC** (*analog-to-digital converter*).

# The 10-bit ADC

The ADC measures the voltage on the pin (from 0 to 5 V) and turns it into a whole number from **0 to 1023**, because it has **10 bits** (2¹⁰ = 1024 values):

- 0 V → 0
- 2.5 V → ~512
- 5 V → 1023

Each "step" is worth 5 V / 1024 ≈ **4.9 mV**. The function is `analogRead(A0)`.

# The potentiometer: a voltage divider

A potentiometer is a resistor with a **wiper** that slides along it. The ends go to 5 V and GND, and the wiper (middle pin) goes to **A0**. It forms a **voltage divider**:

**V_out = 5 V × R₂ / (R₁ + R₂)**

Here R₁ is the part of the track between 5 V and the wiper, and R₂ the part between the wiper and GND. Turning the shaft changes the ratio between R₁ and R₂, and the voltage on the wiper goes from 0 to 5 V.

# Converting scales with map()

`analogRead` gives 0–1023, but `analogWrite` accepts 0–255. The `map` function does the rule of three:

```
int brilho = map(leitura, 0, 1023, 0, 255);
```

"Take `leitura`, which is on the 0–1023 scale, and bring it to the 0–255 scale." It's the same as `leitura * 255 / 1023`, or roughly `leitura / 4`. (*leitura* means "reading" and *brilho* "brightness".)

Careful: `analogWrite` only understands **0 to 255**. If you send the raw value (for example 1023), the result is wrong: on pins 3, 5, 6 and 11 the number "wraps around" (256 becomes 0, 300 becomes 44), and the brightness climbs and drops several times as you turn the potentiometer.
ard-04-potenciometro.task: The potentiometer is on **A0** and the LED on pin **9**. Make the LED's brightness follow the potentiometer: turned all the way to one side → off; to the other → full brightness. Use `analogRead`, `map` and `analogWrite` (and a `delay(20)` at the end of the loop).
hints: int brilho = map(leitura, 0, 1023, 0, 255);
Then: analogWrite(LED, brilho);
Don't send the reading straight to analogWrite: 1023 is much bigger than the maximum of 255.
checks: Potentiometer at zero → LED off
Potentiometer at maximum → full brightness
Potentiometer in the middle → half brightness
The LED follows the potentiometer as it turns

ard-05-serial-ldr.title: Serial Monitor and light sensor (LDR)
ard-05-serial-ldr.theory:
# Talking to the computer: the Serial port

When something doesn't work, how do we know what the Arduino is "thinking"? Through **serial communication**: the Arduino sends text, one bit at a time, over the USB cable, and the computer shows it in the **Serial Monitor**.

```
Serial.begin(9600);        // in setup: starts serial at 9600 bits per second
Serial.print("Luz: ");     // writes without a new line
Serial.println(valor);     // writes and moves to the next line
```

The number **9600** is the speed (*baud rate*) — both sides must use the same one. Without `Serial.begin`, nothing shows up!

# The LDR: a resistor that senses light

The **LDR** (*Light Dependent Resistor*) changes its resistance with light:

- **Lots of light** → **low** resistance (a few kΩ)
- **Dark** → **high** resistance (hundreds of kΩ)

We build a **voltage divider**: the LDR between 5 V and A0, and a fixed 10 kΩ resistor between A0 and GND. In this circuit, the **more light**, the **higher** the `analogRead` reading (close to 1023); in the dark it drops to near 0.

# Making decisions with a threshold

To turn a continuous reading into a decision (bright/dark), we choose a **threshold**:

```
if (luz < 300) {
  // it's dark
} else {
  // it's bright
}
```

That's the principle of an **automatic night light**, like street lamps.
ard-05-serial-ldr.task:
The LDR is on **A0** and an LED on pin **13**. Every **500 ms**: read the light, print a line `Luz: <value>` to the Serial Monitor and, on the next line, `escuro` (if the reading is below **300**) or `claro`. When it is dark, turn the LED on; when it is bright, turn it off.

(*Luz* = light, *escuro* = dark, *claro* = bright. Print these exact words — the checker looks for them.)
hints: Without Serial.begin(9600); in setup() nothing appears in the Serial Monitor.
Serial.print("Luz: "); followed by Serial.println(luz); writes everything on the same line and breaks the line at the end.
if (luz < 300) { Serial.println("escuro"); digitalWrite(LED, HIGH); } else { ... }
checks: Prints "Luz: 800" when the room is bright
Writes "claro" when there is light
The LED stays off when it is bright
Prints "Luz: 100" in the dark
Writes "escuro" when light is missing
The LED turns on in the dark

ard-07-servo.title: Servo motor: sweeping from 0° to 180°
ard-07-servo.theory:
# What is a servo

A **servo motor** (like the SG90) doesn't spin endlessly: it goes to an **angle** you send, between **0° and 180°**, and holds that position. Inside it has a small DC motor, gears and a **potentiometer** that measures the shaft position — a small **closed-loop control** system: it compares where it is with where it should be and corrects.

# How we send the angle

The servo has 3 wires: brown (GND), red (5 V) and orange (**signal**). The signal is a pulse repeated every 20 ms; the **pulse width** sets the angle:

- ~0.5 ms → 0°
- ~1.5 ms → 90°
- ~2.4 ms → 180°

(The Servo library uses 544 µs to 2400 µs; each servo model varies a little.) We don't need to generate this by hand: the **Servo** library does it all. One detail: it uses the chip's **Timer1**, so while a servo is attached, `analogWrite` stops working on pins **9 and 10**.

```
#include <Servo.h>

Servo motor;            // creates a servo object

void setup() {
  motor.attach(9);      // the signal is on pin 9
}

void loop() {
  motor.write(90);      // go to 90 degrees
}
```

Notice the `motor.write(...)` syntax: the dot calls a **function of the object** (this comes from C++, which the Arduino uses).

# Speed

An SG90 takes about **0.1 s to turn 60°**. If we send angles too fast, it can't keep up. That's why, in a **sweep**, we move 1° at a time with a pause of ~15 ms: 180 steps × 15 ms ≈ 2.7 s to go from one side to the other.

Servos like this move model-plane rudders, robot arms, parking barriers and the "head" of robots that look for obstacles.
ard-07-servo.task: The servo is on pin **9**. Make a sweep: from **0° to 180°**, one degree at a time with `delay(15)`, and then from **180° back to 0°** the same way, forever.
hints: for (int angulo = 0; angulo <= 180; angulo++) { motor.write(angulo); delay(15); }
To go back, count down: for (int angulo = 180; angulo >= 0; angulo--) { ... }
The object is called motor, so the commands are motor.attach(9) and motor.write(angulo).
checks: At 0.75 s the servo is near 50° (rising)
Around 2.7 s it reaches 180°
At 4 s it is on its way back, near 95°
Around 5.4 s it is back at 0°

ard-09-motor-dc.title: DC motor with an H-bridge: speed, direction and LCD
ard-09-motor-dc.theory:
# Why the Arduino doesn't drive a motor directly

An Arduino pin can take at most **40 mA** (the recommended limit is 20 mA). A small DC motor draws **hundreds of mA** (and much more when starting). Wiring it directly would burn the pin. Besides, the motor is a **coil**: when switched off, it produces voltage spikes that can damage the chip. That's why a motor always gets **freewheeling diodes** (*flyback*), which give that current a safe path — L298N modules already have these diodes on the board.

# The H-bridge (L298N)

The **H-bridge** is a circuit with 4 switches (transistors) arranged like an "H", with the motor in the middle. Closing the switches diagonally, current flows through the motor **one way or the other** — and it comes from a separate power supply, not from the Arduino (the L298N "eats" about 2 V of that supply). On the **L298N** module:

- IN1 = `HIGH`, IN2 = `LOW` → turns **forward**
- IN1 = `LOW`, IN2 = `HIGH` → turns **backward** (reverse)
- IN1 and IN2 equal → the motor **stops** (brakes)

The **EN** (*enable*) pin switches the bridge on. Sending **PWM** to it with `analogWrite(EN, v)`, we control the **speed**: the average voltage on the motor is proportional to v/255 (it's the same PWM as the LED!).

# Detecting the press (edge), not "being pressed"

We want **each press** of the button to reverse the direction. If we write only `if (digitalRead(BOTAO) == LOW) frente = !frente;`, while the finger is on the button the `loop` runs dozens of times and the direction keeps flipping nonstop! The right way is to detect the **falling edge**: the button **was** released (HIGH) and **now** is pressed (LOW):

```
int botao = digitalRead(BOTAO);
if (botaoAnterior == HIGH && botao == LOW) {
  frente = !frente;          // ! inverts: true becomes false and vice versa
}
botaoAnterior = botao;
```

Real buttons also **bounce**: when pressed, the contact opens and closes several times within a few milliseconds. The `delay(50)` at the end of the loop makes the program read the button only every 50 ms, so those bounces don't turn into several presses — it's a simple *debounce*.

(*botao* = button, *botaoAnterior* = previous button, *frente* = forward.)

# The 16x2 LCD display

The **LiquidCrystal** library drives displays with 2 lines × 16 columns:

```
LiquidCrystal lcd(12, 11, 10, 9, 4, 3);   // pins RS, E, D4, D5, D6, D7
lcd.begin(16, 2);       // in setup
lcd.setCursor(0, 1);    // column 0, line 1 (the bottom one)
lcd.print("Ola!");
```

Tip: when rewriting a number that may get shorter (from 100 to 99), print a few spaces after it to erase the leftover digit.
ard-09-motor-dc.task:
Motor on the L298N: **IN1 = 8**, **IN2 = 7**, **EN = 5**. Potentiometer on **A0** and button (with `INPUT_PULLUP`) on pin **2**. 16x2 LCD with `LiquidCrystal lcd(12, 11, 10, 9, 4, 3)`.

1. The speed (0–255) comes from the potentiometer (use `map`).
2. Each **press** of the button reverses the direction (start going forward).
3. LCD line 0: `Vel: <speed>`; line 1: `Frente` or `Re`.
4. End the loop with `delay(50)`.

(*Vel* = speed, *Frente* = forward, *Re* = reverse. Show these exact texts — the checker looks for them.)

On the LCD: lcd.setCursor(0, 0); lcd.print("Vel: "); lcd.print(velocidade); — and on line 1 write "Frente" or "Re    " (with spaces to erase the old letters).

The LCD shows "Vel: 255"
The LCD shows "Frente"
Potentiometer at zero → motor stopped

The LCD shows "Re" after the press
A second press goes back to forward (one press = one change)

ard-10-robo-seguidor.title: Line-following robot with P control and obstacle stop
ard-10-robo-seguidor.theory:
# The robot

Our robot has **differential drive**: two wheels, each with its own DC motor, connected to an L298N H-bridge, and a free caster wheel at the front. To turn, one wheel spins faster than the other — like a tank.

- **Left** motor: IN1 = 8, IN2 = 7, ENA = 5 (PWM)
- **Right** motor: IN3 = 4, IN4 = 2, ENB = 6 (PWM)
- **Ultrasonic** sensor at the front: TRIG = 10, ECHO = 11
- Two **line sensors** (infrared, TCRT5000 type) looking at the floor, one to the left and one to the right of the line: **A0** (left) and **A1** (right)

# How the line sensor sees

The sensor emits infrared light and measures how much comes back. The **white** floor **reflects** a lot; the **black** tape **absorbs** it. On this robot, `analogRead` gives about **80 on white** and reaches about **950 on top of the black line**, with in-between values at the edge.

# On-off control vs. proportional control

The simplest idea is: "line to the left? turn left all the way". It works, but the robot **zigzags** — it over-corrects, overshoots and corrects again.

**Proportional (P) control** corrects **in proportion to the error**:

```
erro = esquerdo - direito;          // > 0: the line is more to the left
correcao = KP * erro;
velocidadeEsquerda = BASE - correcao;
velocidadeDireita  = BASE + correcao;
```

(*erro* = error, *correcao* = correction, *esquerdo/direito* = left/right, *velocidade* = speed.)

- Robot centered → both sensors read the same → error 0 → drives straight.
- Line pulling to the left → the left sensor reads more → positive error → the **right wheel speeds up** and the left one slows down → the robot turns left, back onto the line.

The gain **KP** is "how strongly to react": too small and the robot leaves the line in the curves; too big and it oscillates. With errors of up to ~870 and a base of 150, **KP ≈ 0.15** gives corrections of up to ~130 — a good start. In real robotics, the **I** (integral) and **D** (derivative) terms are added too: that's the famous **PID control**.

# Safety first: obstacles

Before each correction, the robot measures the distance ahead with the ultrasonic sensor. If something is **closer than 15 cm**, it **stops both motors** and does nothing else in that pass of the `loop` (`return;`). This way it never crashes.

# Organizing the code

A function `motor(in1, in2, en, velocidade)` that accepts speeds **from −255 to 255** (negative = reverse) keeps `loop()` short and readable. Use `constrain(v, -255, 255)` to never go past the limit.

Tip: in `pulseIn`, pass a time limit (`pulseIn(ECHO, HIGH, 30000)`): without it, when there is no echo `pulseIn` may wait up to 1 s, and the robot is "blind" and out of control during that time. With the time limit it returns 0 — and the distance function treats 0 as "nothing ahead".
ard-10-robo-seguidor.task: Complete the robot so that it **follows the black line to the goal** using **proportional control** with sensors A0 (left) and A1 (right): base speed **150**, **KP = 0.15**, `erro = esquerdo - direito`, left wheel = base − correction, right wheel = base + correction. Before correcting, measure the distance with the ultrasonic sensor: if it is **less than 15 cm**, stop both motors. End the loop with `delay(5)`.
hints: Create long distanciaCm() just like the one in the ultrasonic lesson (with pulseIn(ECHO, HIGH, 30000) and returning 999 when the result is 0).
At the start of loop: if (distanciaCm() < 15) { motor(IN1, IN2, ENA, 0); motor(IN3, IN4, ENB, 0); return; }
P control: int erro = analogRead(A0) - analogRead(A1); int correcao = 0.15 * erro; left motor with 150 - correcao and right with 150 + correcao.
checks: The robot follows the line and reaches the goal
The robot stays on top of the line for most of the way
The robot doesn't hit anything
With an obstacle on the line, the robot stops
…and stops without hitting the obstacle

ard-11-debounce.title: Debounce: counting presses without mistakes
ard-11-debounce.theory:
# The button that "bounces"

A button looks perfect: press, it connects; release, it disconnects. But inside there are two metal blades that hit each other — and, like a rubber ball, they **bounce** a few times before settling. For 1 to 10 milliseconds the contact opens and closes several times.

To us that is invisible. To the Arduino, which reads the pin **thousands of times per second**, a single press becomes a burst:

```
pressed ─┐ ┌─┐ ┌───────────────
         └─┘ └─┘
         ←  ~8 ms →
```

A program that counts "every time the pin went LOW" counts **3 or 4 presses** instead of 1. If the button toggles a lamp, it flickers and may end in the wrong state.

# Detecting the edge

Before debouncing, remember the idea of an **edge**: we want the *moment* the button goes from released to pressed, not "while it is pressed". We keep the previous reading and compare:

```
if (leitura == LOW && anterior == HIGH) { /* just pressed */ }
anterior = leitura;
```

# Time-based debounce

The classic solution (the one in the official Arduino example) is to **distrust any change** until it has stayed still for a while — typically **50 ms**:

1. Every time the reading **changes**, note `ultimaMudanca = millis()`.
2. Only accept the reading as the new **stable state** when `millis() - ultimaMudanca >= 50`.
3. Count the press when the **stable** state goes from HIGH to LOW.

These are two different variables: `ultimaLeitura` (what the pin showed in the previous pass, bounces and all) and `estadoEstavel` (what we decided is true). Note there is **no `delay()`**: `loop()` keeps spinning freely, ready to do other things.

# Other ways to solve it

- **Hardware:** a 100 nF capacitor across the button forms an RC filter that "smooths" the bounces (with a Schmitt trigger it becomes perfect).
- **Sample counter:** only accept the change after N equal readings in a row.
- `delay(50)` after detecting the press also works, but it **freezes** the program — and you already know why that is bad.
ard-11-debounce.task: The button is on pin **2** (with `INPUT_PULLUP`) and the LED on **13**. The starter code counts presses, but every bounce of the contact becomes an extra press. Fix it with a **50 ms debounce using `millis()`**: on each real press add 1, **toggle the LED** and show `Apertos: N` on the Serial Monitor.
hints: Create the variables ultimaLeitura, estadoEstavel (both starting at HIGH) and unsigned long ultimaMudanca = 0.
If leitura != ultimaLeitura, do ultimaMudanca = millis(). At the end of loop, ultimaLeitura = leitura.
Only count when millis() - ultimaMudanca >= 50 AND leitura != estadoEstavel: then update estadoEstavel and, if it is LOW, count the press.
checks: Without pressing, nothing is counted
A bouncy press counts as 1
…and not as 2
The LED toggles (turns on) on the first press
Two bouncy presses count 2
…and not 3 or more
The second press turns the LED off again

ard-12-multitarefa.title: Multitasking with millis(): several things at once
ard-12-multitarefa.theory:
# One processor, several tasks

The Arduino Uno has **a single core** and no operating system. Even so, real robots do many things "at the same time": they blink status LEDs, read sensors, drive motors, talk over serial. The trick is called **cooperative multitasking**: each task does a quick little piece of its work and **gives the turn back**, and `loop()` passes through all of them thousands of times per second.

The golden rule: **no task may use `delay()`**. A `delay(250)` freezes every other task for 250 ms.

# The "is it time yet?" pattern

Each periodic task gets its own time variable:

```
unsigned long ultimoRapido = 0;

if (millis() - ultimoRapido >= 250) {
  ultimoRapido += 250;          // schedule the next one
  // ...do the task (toggle the LED)
}
```

Note the `ultimoRapido += 250` instead of `ultimoRapido = millis()`. If loop is 3 ms late in one pass, `= millis()` pushes all the following events 3 ms forward and the error **accumulates** (the clock "drifts"). With `+= 250` the next event stays on the right grid: 250, 500, 750… This matters in everything that measures time — clocks, sample rates, controllers.

# Independent tasks

This circuit has three tasks:

- **Task 1:** toggles the LED on pin 13 every **250 ms**.
- **Task 2:** toggles the LED on pin 12 every **400 ms**.
- **Task 3:** copies the button on pin 2 to the LED on pin 11, **all the time**.

Since 250 and 400 are not multiples of each other, there is **no way** to do this with `delay()`s in sequence. With `millis()` it is trivial: three independent `if`s in the same `loop()`.

# How far does this go?

This is the same principle as the **schedulers** of embedded systems and *event loops* (JavaScript, games). When the tasks get too heavy, an **RTOS** (real-time operating system, such as FreeRTOS) is used: it switches tasks by itself on a timer interrupt — but the "never block" idea still holds.

ard-13-rampa-pwm.title: Acceleration ramp: soft-starting a motor
ard-13-rampa-pwm.theory:
# Why not switch it on at full power?

A stopped DC motor has no **back-EMF** (the voltage it generates while spinning, which opposes the supply). At the instant it starts, the only thing limiting the current is the winding resistance, a few ohms: the starting current can be **5 to 10 times** the rated one. That drags the battery voltage down (the Arduino may reset!), heats the H-bridge and gives a mechanical **jolt** that wears gears and makes the robot skid or pop a wheelie.

The solution is a **ramp**: increase the PWM little by little.

# Trapezoidal ramp

The most common profile has three phases — the speed graph looks like a trapezoid:

```
PWM 255 |      ________
        |     /        \
        |    /          \
      0 |___/            \______
        0   1 s        3 s  4 s
       accelerate cruise brake
```

During the ramp, the PWM is a **linear interpolation** of time:

```
pwm = t · 255 / 1000          (0 ≤ t < 1000 ms)
```

At 500 ms the motor is at 127 (half); at 1000 ms it reaches 255. Braking is the same calculation "in reverse": `pwm = (4000 − t) · 255 / 1000`.

The **acceleration** is the slope of the ramp: 255 units per second. A slower ramp draws less current and is smoother; a faster one responds better. The designer picks it from the driver's current limit and from how much the wheels can take without skidding (**static friction**: a = μ·g is the most a robot can accelerate without slipping).

# Watch the types

`t * 255` with `t` in milliseconds can exceed 32 767 — the limit of an `int` on the Arduino Uno. Use `unsigned long` (up to ~4.3 billion) in calculations with `millis()`.

# Going further: the S-curve

In the trapezoidal ramp the acceleration jumps from **zero to maximum** suddenly — that is a "jerk" (in physics, *jerk* is the derivative of acceleration). Elevators, CNC machines and 3D printers use **S-curve ramps**, in which the acceleration itself also rises and falls smoothly. Same idea, one derivative higher.

Use `millis()` to compute the PWM on every pass of `loop()`.

ard-14-protocolo-serial.title: Serial protocol: commands from the computer
ard-14-protocolo-serial.theory:
# Talking to the Arduino

So far the Serial Monitor was output only. But serial communication (UART) goes **both ways**: the computer — or a Raspberry Pi, a Bluetooth module, another microcontroller — can **send commands**. That is how a dashboard controls a robot, how a 3D printer receives G-code, how a drone receives orders.

For that we need a **protocol**: rules both sides agree on. Ours is text-based, one line per command:

- `LIGA` → brightness 255, replies `OK`
- `DESLIGA` → brightness 0, replies `OK`
- `BRILHO n` → brightness n (0 to 255), replies `OK` — or `ERRO: valor` if n doesn't fit
- `STATUS` → changes nothing, replies `BRILHO=n`
- anything else → replies `ERRO: comando`

(The commands are in Portuguese: *liga* = on, *desliga* = off, *brilho* = brightness, *erro* = error.)

# Bytes arrive bit by bit

Serial delivers **one character at a time**, and they don't all arrive together: at 9600 baud each byte takes ~1 ms, and a command may arrive split across two passes of `loop()`. That's why we **store** the characters in a **buffer** until the terminator `'\n'` (end of line) arrives:

```
while (Serial.available() > 0) {
  char c = Serial.read();
  if (c == '\n') { buffer[tamanho] = '\0'; executar(buffer); tamanho = 0; }
  else if (tamanho < 31) { buffer[tamanho] = c; tamanho++; }
}
```

The `'\0'` at the end turns the array into a **C string**. The `tamanho < 31` test protects against **buffer overflow** — a giant line must not write past the array (on computers, that bug has brought down many systems and is a classic door for attacks).

# Interpreting (parsing)

With the complete line, we compare using the `<string.h>` functions:

- `strcmp(a, b) == 0` → the strings are equal.
- `strncmp(cmd, "BRILHO ", 7) == 0` → the command **starts** with "BRILHO ".
- `atoi(cmd + 7)` → converts the text from the 8th character on into a number. `cmd + 7` is **pointer arithmetic**: the address 7 positions ahead.

# Validation

Never trust what comes from outside! `BRILHO 300` doesn't fit in an 8-bit PWM: the protocol must **refuse** it (`ERRO: valor`) instead of applying a wrong value. Always replying (`OK` or `ERRO`) lets the other side know whether the command worked — that is an **acknowledgment**, the basis of reliable protocols.

ard-15-histerese.title: Averaging filter and hysteresis: a smart street light
ard-15-histerese.theory:
# The street light that flickers

An automatic street light uses an LDR: dark, it turns on; bright, it turns off. The first idea is a single **threshold**:

```
if (luz < 400) acende(); else apaga();
```

At dusk, however, the light stays **close to 400** for several minutes, and any noise (a cloud, a car's headlights, electrical interference) makes the reading cross the threshold back and forth: the lamp **flickers**, the relay clicks, everything wears out. Two problems, two tools.

# 1. Hysteresis: two thresholds

We use **one threshold to turn on and another to turn off**:

- off → only **turns on** when the light drops **below 300**;
- on → only **turns off** when the light rises **above 500**.

Between 300 and 500 the lamp **keeps the state** it was in. The band between the thresholds (the **hysteresis band**) is larger than the noise, so the noise can no longer make the output oscillate. It is the same principle as a fridge **thermostat** and the **Schmitt trigger** component. The system now has **memory**: the output depends on the current value *and* on the previous state — one more state machine!

# 2. Moving average: smoothing the noise

A fast spike (a camera flash, headlights) can still cross both thresholds. For that we **filter** the reading: instead of the raw value, we use the **average of the last N readings**, kept in a **circular buffer**:

```
soma -= leituras[pos];          // remove the oldest
leituras[pos] = analogRead(A0); // put the new one in its place
soma += leituras[pos];
pos = (pos + 1) % N;            // the index "wraps around"
media = soma / N;
```

Keeping `soma` up to date avoids adding the whole array every time. With N = 8 and one reading every 10 ms, the average "sees" the last 80 ms: a 30 ms spike barely moves it, but a real change shows up in less than 0.1 s.

In signal processing this is a **low-pass filter** of the FIR kind: it lets slow variations through and cuts fast ones. The price is a small **delay** in the response — there is always a trade-off between smoothness and speed.

One detail: in `setup()`, **fill the buffer** with the first reading. If it starts with zeros, the average starts at 0 ("pitch dark") and the lamp turns on by itself at power-up.

ard-16-alarme.title: Alarm with a state machine: arm, trigger and disarm
ard-16-alarme.theory:
# A real system

A home alarm looks simple, but it has **rules that depend on the moment**: the same movement in front of the sensor is ignored when the alarm is disarmed and fires the siren when it is armed; the same button arms or disarms. Writing that with loose `if`s turns into a tangle. The professional way is a well-designed **finite state machine** (FSM).

# States and transitions

(The state names are in Portuguese: DESARMADO = disarmed, ARMANDO = arming, ARMADO = armed, DISPARADO = triggered.)

```
            button                3 s
DESARMADO ───────→ ARMANDO ───────────→ ARMADO
    ↑  ↑   button     │                   │ someone < 50 cm
    │  └──────────────┘                   ↓
    └─────────────── button ─────────── DISPARADO
```

- **DESARMADO:** LED and siren off; the sensor is ignored.
- **ARMANDO:** this is the **exit delay** — 3 s for the person to leave home without setting off their own alarm. The LED blinks.
- **ARMADO:** LED on; if the ultrasonic sensor measures less than 50 cm, go to DISPARADO.
- **DISPARADO:** siren (`tone` at 2000 Hz) until someone presses the button.

Drawing the diagram **before** programming is half the work: each arrow becomes an `if` inside the `case` of the state it leaves.

# Entry actions

Some things must happen **once, on entering** a state: reset the timer, report over serial. Put that in one function:

```
void mudarPara(int novo) {
  estado = novo;
  inicio = millis();
  Serial.print("Estado: ");
  // ...print the state's name
}
```

Logging every transition on the Serial Monitor is gold for debugging: you see exactly the sequence the system went through.

# Events, not levels

The button must act on the **press** (the edge), not "while it is pressed" — otherwise, holding the button, the alarm would arm and disarm in turn on every pass. Keep the previous reading and detect the change from HIGH to LOW (with debounce, if the button is real).

# Why this matters

State machines control elevators, traffic lights, network protocols, ATMs, game logic and drone flight modes. They make behavior **verifiable**: you can list every state and check, one by one, that no combination of events leads to a dangerous situation.

On every change print `Estado: ` and the name of the new state (start by printing `Estado: DESARMADO`).

ard-17-seguidor-solar.title: Solar tracker: two sensors, a dead band and a servo
ard-17-seguidor-solar.theory:
# Panels that follow the Sun

A solar panel produces most when the light hits it **head-on**: the power falls with the cosine of the angle of incidence. A **solar tracker** turns the panel during the day and can produce 25 to 35% more than a fixed panel. The simplest sensor for this is **two LDRs** separated by a small wall: if the panel is turned too far to the right, the wall shades the right LDR, and the left one gets more light.

# Measuring the error

The system's **error** is the difference between the two sensors:

```
diferenca = analogRead(A0) - analogRead(A1);   // left − right
```

- `diferenca > 0` → more light on the left → turn left (increase the angle, towards 180°);
- `diferenca < 0` → turn right (decrease it, towards 0°);
- close to 0 → the panel points at the Sun.

# Dead band

Two LDRs are never identical, and light is noisy: the difference is almost never exactly 0. If the servo moved on every tiny difference, it would keep jittering back and forth (wearing the servo and wasting the energy the panel should save). The solution is a **dead band**: **do nothing** while `|diferenca| ≤ 50`. It is a close relative of the hysteresis of the previous lesson.

# Limiting the speed

We don't send the servo straight to 0° or 180°: we move **1 degree every 20 ms** (50°/s), always checking the sensors again. This is an **incremental** (or integral) control: the angle is the *sum* of the small corrections. It stops by itself when the sensors balance — or when it hits the limit, which is why we use `constrain(angulo, 0, 180)`.

Note the difference from the P control of the robot lesson: there the correction was **proportional** to the error; here the servo moves at **constant speed** while there is error outside the dead band. Real controllers often combine both ideas.

# Time without delay

As in the previous lessons, the 20 ms step is timed with `millis()`, leaving `loop()` free — in a real project it would also be reading the battery, showing data on a display, etc.

Keep the angle between 0 and 180.

ard-18-pid-distancia.title: PID control: stopping 20 cm from the wall
ard-18-pid-distancia.theory:
# The problem

The robot is in an empty room, facing the wall, ~2 m away from it. Mission: **arrive and stop exactly 20 cm** from the wall, quickly and without crashing. Sounds easy — until you try.

**Bang-bang** ("drive at full speed until 20 cm, then stop") gets there fast, but the robot has inertia: when the sensor says "20", the motors still take a moment to brake, and it stops **closer** than it should. Against a real wall, or with a heavier robot, that is a crash.

# The PID controller

The **PID** computes the command by adding three terms of the **error** `e = distance − target`:

```
u = KP·e  +  KI·∫e dt  +  KD·de/dt
```

- **P (proportional):** far → fast; close → slow. It is the natural "brake".
- **I (integral):** adds up the error over time. If the robot **gets stuck** with a small error, the integral grows until it beats whatever holds it back.
- **D (derivative):** looks at **how fast** the error changes and brakes before overshooting, damping the motion.

# Why P alone doesn't get there

Our motors have a **dead zone**: with PWM below ~25 the wheel doesn't even move (friction, minimum voltage). With P only, near the target `KP·e` gets smaller than 25 and the robot **stops early**: with KP = 5, it gets stuck at about 25 cm. That is the famous **steady-state error**. Raising KP reduces the error but doesn't remove it (and, on real robots, makes it oscillate). What zeroes the error is the **I**: while there is error left, the integral grows.

# Anti-windup

The integral has a flaw: during the approach, with errors of 150 cm for several seconds, it becomes **huge** (*windup*), and the robot overshoots the target while it "empties". The fix is simple: **only integrate near the target** (here, when |e| < 10 cm) and reset the integral outside that band.

# Discrete implementation

The microcontroller computes the PID at instants separated by `dt` (here 20 ms, i.e. 50 Hz):

```
integral += erro * dt;
derivada = (erro - erroAnterior) / dt;
erroAnterior = erro;
u = KP * erro + KI * integral + KD * derivada;
```

Measure `dt` for real with `millis()` and remember to start `erroAnterior` with the first error — otherwise the first derivative gives a huge "kick". Finally, limit the command (`constrain(u, -200, 200)`): it becomes the speed and direction of both wheels (negative = reverse, if it overshoots).

**Tuning:** start with P only until the robot approaches well; add D if it overshoots; add I until the final error disappears. The values KP = 12, KI = 4 and KD = 1 work well for this robot.

ard-19-odometria.title: Odometry: the kinematics of the differential-drive robot
ard-19-odometria.theory:
# Navigating without seeing

There isn't always a line on the floor. Warehouse robots, robot vacuums and rovers estimate where they are by counting **how far each wheel has turned**: that is **odometry**. Here we'll do the simplest version — **by time** —, computing how long each movement must last.

# The motor model

Measuring our robot on a straight line, we found:

- below PWM **25** the wheel doesn't turn (dead zone);
- with PWM **255** the wheel reaches **40 cm/s**;
- in between, the speed grows in a straight line:

```
v = (PWM − 25) / 230 × 40      [cm/s]
```

With PWM 150: v = 125 / 230 × 40 ≈ **21.7 cm/s**.

# Differential kinematics

With speeds `vE` (left) and `vD` (right) and **track width** `b` (the distance between the wheels, here **12 cm**):

```
v = (vE + vD) / 2          speed of the robot's center
ω = (vE − vD) / b          turning speed (rad/s)
```

- **Straight line:** vE = vD = v → ω = 0. To travel a distance d: `t = d / v`. For 50 cm: 50 / 21.7 ≈ **2.30 s**.
- **Turning in place:** vE = −v and vD = +v → the center stays put and each wheel runs on a circle of radius b/2. To turn an angle θ, each wheel travels the arc `(b/2)·θ`, so `t = (b/2)·θ / v`. For 90° (θ = π/2): 6 · 1.571 / 21.7 ≈ **0.434 s**.

Left wheel backward and right wheel forward turns the robot to the **left**.

# A mission plan

Instead of a giant `if`, we describe the path as **data**: an array of steps, each with the speed of both wheels and the duration.

```
struct Passo { int esquerda; int direita; unsigned long duracao; };
```

`loop()` just runs the current step and, when its time is up, moves to the next one. To draw another shape, just change the plan — the program's "engine" stays the same. The 300 ms **pauses** between movements let the robot stop completely, so that one movement doesn't "contaminate" the next.

# The limits of odometry

Slipping tires, one wheel slightly bigger than the other, a draining battery… every small error **accumulates** at every step — and angle errors turn into ever-larger position errors. That is why real robots use wheel **encoders**, gyroscopes and, from time to time, correct their position with external landmarks (lines, cameras, GPS): that is **sensor fusion**.

ard-20-missao-final.title: Final mission: avoid the obstacle and get back to the line
ard-20-missao-final.theory:
# Putting it all together

This is the graduation mission of the track. The robot of lesson 10 **stopped** in front of an obstacle. Now it must **go around it, find the line again and finish the course** — and stop by itself when the line ends. You'll use almost everything you've learned: P control, ultrasonic sensor, `millis()`, state machine and differential kinematics.

# The mission's state machine

(The state names are in Portuguese: SEGUINDO = following, GIRA_ESQ = turn left, CONTORNA = go around, GIRA_DIR = turn right, PROCURA = search, FIM = end.)

- **SEGUINDO:** P control on the line (base 150, KP = 0.15). If the ultrasonic sensor reads **less than 15 cm** → GIRA_ESQ. If **both sensors** see only white floor (< 200) → FIM: the line is over.
- **GIRA_ESQ:** turns left in place (wheels −150 and 150) for **300 ms**.
- **CONTORNA:** drives straight for **1800 ms**, passing beside the obstacle.
- **GIRA_DIR:** turns right for **430 ms**, pointing back towards the line.
- **PROCURA:** drives slowly (130) until **one** of the sensors goes above **500** → SEGUINDO.
- **FIM:** motors stopped. Mission accomplished.

The maneuver times are **odometry** (previous lesson): with PWM 150 the robot turns ~207°/s and drives ~21.7 cm/s. The maneuver draws a "step" over the obstacle; it doesn't need to be perfect, because the **PROCURA** state and the P control fix whatever is left. That combination — a rough plan plus a sensor that closes the loop — is the heart of mobile robotics.

# Details that make a difference

- **Order of the tests in SEGUINDO:** first the end of the line, then the obstacle. At the end of the course there is a wall right ahead; if the robot tested for the obstacle first, it would try to "go around" the wall.
- **Hysteresis on the sensors:** "found the line" is **> 500**, but "the line is over" is **< 200**. With a single threshold, a sensor on the edge of the tape (reading ~500) would make the state jump back and forth.
- **`mudarPara()`** resets each state's timer, as in the traffic light and the alarm.

# What next?

Competition robots swap P for **PID**, timed maneuvers for **encoders** and the fixed detour for a **wall follower** that goes around obstacles of any size. Self-driving cars do the same thing on a giant scale: **perception → planning → control**, in a state machine that decides whether the car follows the lane, overtakes or stops. You have just built a pocket version of that.
